analysis.one_liner: Caps drug costs by extending Medicare price negotiation to private insurance and limiting out-of-pocket spending.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 59 House Democrats behind it, the bill sits in three committees with no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would extend the Medicare program that negotiates drug prices — from 20 drugs a year to 50 — so that the negotiated prices also apply to drugs sold through private and employer insurance, not just Medicare. It would require drug makers to pay back price increases that outpace inflation on drugs sold in the commercial market, roll back recent changes that weakened the negotiation program, and cap what people with private insurance pay out of pocket for drugs at $2,000 a year, with insulin capped at $35 a month and no deductible for covered insulins. It would also restore essential-benefit requirements for individual and small-group plans.
analysis.who_benefits: People with private, employer-sponsored, or Medicare drug coverage. The bill would let Medicare's negotiated prices follow a drug into the commercial market [S2], cap annual out-of-pocket drug spending for privately insured people at $2,000 (2027, rising with premiums after) [S2], cap insulin cost-sharing at $35 per 30-day supply with no deductible for covered insulin products [S2], reinstate overall out-of-pocket limits and essential health benefits for individual and small-group plans [S2], and restore provisions of the negotiation program that a 2025 law changed [S2]. Medicare enrollees benefit too: more drugs negotiated each year, international prices considered in negotiations starting 2028, and recent changes to the program repealed [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Privately insured people and Medicare enrollees

how_it_helps.text: Increases the number of drugs Medicare negotiates each year from 20 to 50 and requires negotiators to consider the average prices paid in Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Japan, and the United Kingdom for negotiations beginning in 2028 [S2].

Lets private and employer health plans participate in the Medicare negotiation program by default — plans must affirmatively opt out, and any opt-out is published — so negotiated 'maximum fair prices' and the caps on cost-sharing apply to drugs covered by those plans [S2].
Applies Medicare's inflation rebates, which claw back drug price increases above inflation, to drugs furnished in the commercial market, not just drugs billed to Medicare [S2].

Caps annual prescription-drug out-of-pocket spending for private insurance at $2,000 for individual coverage starting in 2027 (twice that for family coverage), caps insulin cost-sharing at $35 per 30-day supply with no deductible, and restores essential health benefits and overall out-of-pocket limits for individual and small-group plans [S2].
Repeals the section of Public Law 119-21 that changed the drug price negotiation program, restoring the program as it was before that law [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers bear the direct cost, through negotiated prices on far more drugs, inflation rebates on commercial-market sales, and international reference prices in negotiations [S2]. Health insurers and employers sponsoring group plans would administer the negotiated prices and cost-sharing caps and could opt out only by public election [S2]; to the extent plans absorb these costs, some may offset them in premiums. Insurance issuers would also have to cover the essential health benefits package in individual and small-group markets again [S2].

drawbacks.text: Participation by private plans is not mandatory: a plan or issuer can opt out of the negotiated prices for a given drug and period, and while the election must be published, the opt-out leaves a door open for plans to sidestep the caps [S2].

The cost-sharing caps and restored essential-benefit requirements apply to employers and insurers, who may pass the added costs back to workers and customers through higher premiums, and the bill sets these mandates without a visible funding mechanism [S2].
The caps and negotiated prices begin in 2027 at the earliest, so no relief arrives before then even if the bill became law quickly [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to households is direct and large: a $2,000 annual cap on drug costs, $35 insulin, and Medicare-negotiated prices extended into the private market address the most common ways people get hit by drug prices. The honest cost is that drug makers would lose substantial revenue on their best-selling drugs, and plans and employers would face new compliance costs that could show up in premiums — and because plans can opt out of the negotiated prices, the protection is strong on paper but partially dependent on plans staying in. The industry argument that lower drug revenue reduces investment in future medicines is a real tradeoff, but it is the same tradeoff every price-negotiation law makes, and the bill phases most of it in starting in 2027-2028.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on November 20, 2025 and referred to three House committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Workforce — and nothing has happened since: no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on November 20, 2025, joined by Reps. Neal and Scott of Virginia as original cosponsors [S2].
The Speaker referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and also to Ways and Means and Education and Workforce, to be split among them later [S4].
Fifty-eight additional members have cosponsored; all 59 total sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats [S3].
The only recorded action since introduction is the committee referral; no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet — the bill has gone nowhere. If it stalls in committee the way single-party drug pricing bills typically do in this House, brand-name drug makers and plan sponsors come out ahead, keeping the current pricing system and the changes made by the 2025 law that this bill would repeal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; stalling would favor drug makers

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 59 sponsors and cosponsors is a Democrat; no Republican has signed on, and the Republican-controlled House has not scheduled any action on it [S3, S4].

industries.note: The bill negotiates prices on 50 drugs a year instead of 20, extends those negotiated prices into the commercial market, applies inflation rebates to private-market sales, and uses prices from six other countries as a benchmark — a direct hit to manufacturers' revenue on their most profitable products [S2]. It also repeals changes the 2025 tax-and-spending law made to the negotiation program [S2].

Insurers must apply Medicare-negotiated prices and cost-sharing caps to covered drugs, restore essential health benefits, and can opt out only through a published election [S2]. They gain a predictable, lower input price on participating drugs but face new mandates and admin costs.

Employer plans fall under the same negotiated-price and cost-sharing caps, with the same published opt-out option [S2]. They save on drug costs if they stay in the program, but bear compliance costs and could opt out to avoid them.

The insulin provision counts all price concessions — including those taken by third parties like PBMs — when calculating the $35 cost-sharing limit, narrowing the spread PBMs can keep on covered insulins [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With a November 2025 introduction, a three-way committee referral, no scheduled action, and zero Republican support in a House run by a Republican majority, the likely path is the usual one for single-party health bills at this stage: it sits in committee and expires at the end of the 119th Congress in January 2027 without a vote. Its realistic best case is being folded into a larger Democratic health package if one ever reaches the floor.
